title: Acquire Infrastructure: Domains
summary: Adversaries register or otherwise obtain domain names so that later stages of an operation have a stable, trustworthy-looking place to send victims. A domain can be bought outright, obtained free from a low-cost registrar, or taken over after it expires. Attackers pick names that resemble a real brand through typosquatting, homoglyphs in other character sets, or a different top-level domain, and they may serve one-time hostnames so each victim sees a unique URL. Repurposed expired domains are attractive because a defender's allowlist or reputation score may already trust them. Registration leaves public artefacts: WHOIS records, registrar and privacy-proxy data, name server choices, certificate transparency log entries, and passive DNS history. Defenders separate hostile domains from legitimate marketing or regional domains by correlating young registration age, privacy shielding, lookalike spelling, certificate issuance patterns, and rapid resolution churn, then confirming with the content served or the traffic direction that follows.

beginner.definition: A domain is the readable name of a website, such as example[.]com. Attackers buy or take over domains before an attack so they have a place on the internet to send victims. This technique is about getting those names ready. It happens long before anything reaches your network.
beginner.whyItMatters: People trust names, not numbers. A name that is almost the same as your bank or your company can fool careful users. Attackers also need long-lived domains to keep controlling infected machines. If your team never watches new domain registrations, the first sign of trouble is usually an employee already clicking the link.
howItWorks: The attacker picks a target brand and creates a name that looks close to it, changing one letter or the ending.
They pay a registrar, a company that sells names, often using a privacy service that hides the real owner.
They point the name at servers they control by editing DNS records, the entries that map names to addresses.
They obtain a digital certificate so browsers show a padlock, which makes the fake site look official.
Expired trusted names may be bought cheaply, because old reputation still follows the name.
Attackers may generate many unique hostnames so each victim gets a link used only once.
beginner.example: Imagine a delivery company called FastParcel. A criminal opens an office nearby and puts up a sign reading FastParcel, with a small change in spelling. Customers walk in and hand over their parcels and their card details. The shop is fake, but the sign looks right, and the building was once a real shop that closed years ago.
takeaways: A familiar-looking name and a padlock do not prove a website is safe.
New or recently renewed domains deserve extra suspicion when they copy your brand.
Watching certificate and domain registration data gives early warning before users click.

objectives: Explain what this sub-technique adds compared with the parent Acquire Infrastructure technique.
Describe how lookalike and expired domains are used to gain victim trust.
Identify the registration and certificate artefacts that reveal a hostile domain.
Distinguish a malicious lookalike domain from a legitimate regional or campaign domain.
Describe the detection data sources that support proactive domain monitoring.
